claims.text: In situ TEM heating can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles as a function of particle size.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit a size-dependent thermal response.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles begin phase or morphological transformations at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
The as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have clean surfaces.
The as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are size-controlled and have narrow size distributions.
Real-time TEM imaging and electron diffraction can identify the onset of thermal phase transformations or morphological changes in individual nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have higher surface-to-volume ratios than larger nanoparticles.
Higher surface-to-volume ratios produce stronger surface-energy effects and enhanced atomic mobility.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher fraction of atoms at or near their surfaces.
A higher fraction of surface atoms lowers the effective energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
A higher fraction of surface atoms lowers the effective energy barrier for phase transformation.
Surface-dominated regions trigger phase transformation or morphological evolution earlier in smaller particles than in larger particles during heating.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles remain thermally stable to higher temperatures than smaller nanoparticles.
Potential thermally induced changes include sintering, grain growth, phase segregation, and phase transitions.
Bulk or larger-scale HEA materials typically have higher transformation temperatures than nanoparticles.
The higher transformation temperatures of bulk or larger-scale HEA materials arise from lower relative surface-energy effects.
Oxidation or contamination can introduce reactions that mask intrinsic size-dependent thermal effects.
The magnitude of transformation-temperature shifts and the identity of the phase changes depend on synthesis and experimental conditions.

contradictions.description: The phrase in predicted_outcome that onset temperature 'decreases with nanoparticle size' literally implies a lower onset as size increases, whereas the hypothesis, mechanism, remainder of the predicted outcome, and falsification rule state that smaller particles have lower onset temperatures. The intended direction is apparent but should be rewritten as 'decreases with decreasing nanoparticle size.'
